# EXC 3420 — Exam-Calibrated Practice Bank

> [!info] How to Use This Practice Bank
> These 12 practice tasks mirror the exact 3-part structure of the **EXC 3420 Wiseflow Final Exam** (**Part 1**: Multiple Choice; **Part 2**: 200-word Short Answers with numerical calculations; **Part 3**: Multi-part Analytical & Graphical Cases).
> - **All answers are collapsed by default** (`> [!question]-`) so you can test yourself first.

## Part 1: Multiple-Choice Practice (1 point each, 1 correct option)

### Question 1 — Topic 1 (Inequality & Production Functions)
In a country, the richest $10\%$ of the population has an average annual income of $1,200,000\text{ NOK}$, while the poorest $10\%$ has an average annual income of $150,000\text{ NOK}$. Suppose every inhabitant in both groups receives an unconditional cash transfer of $+30,000\text{ NOK}$. Which statement is **correct**?
- **A)** The rich/poor ratio remains unchanged at $8.0$ because both groups received the exact same amount in kroner.
- **B)** The rich/poor ratio decreases from $8.0$ to $6.83$.
- **C)** The rich/poor ratio increases because the absolute income gap in kroner increases.
- **D)** The rich/poor ratio only changes if both groups' incomes grow by the same percentage.

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 1)
> **Correct Option: B)**
> - **Initial rich/poor ratio**: $\frac{1,200,000}{150,000} = \mathbf{8.0}$.
> - **After adding $+30,000\text{ NOK}$ to both**: $\frac{1,230,000}{180,000} = \mathbf{6.833} < 8.0$.
> - **Why**: Adding an equal absolute amount in kroner represents a $+20\%$ increase for the poorest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/150\text{k}$) vs. only $+2.5\%$ for the richest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/1,200\text{k}$), lowering the ratio. (Equal *percentage* changes leave the ratio unchanged.)

---

### Question 2 — Topic 2 (Isocost Lines & Technology Choice)
A firm uses labour ($L$, horizontal axis, wage $w = 400\text{ NOK/hour}$) and energy ($R$, vertical axis, price $p = 200\text{ NOK/unit}$). Which statement about the firm's isocost lines is **correct**?
- **A)** The slope of the isocost lines is $-0.5$, and Technologies $A(4, 10)$ and $B(6, 6)$ lie on the same isocost line.
- **B)** The slope of the isocost lines is $-2.0$, and Technologies $A(4, 10)$ and $B(6, 6)$ lie on the same isocost line with total cost $3,600\text{ NOK}$.
- **C)** Technology $B(6, 6)$ dominates Technology $A(4, 10)$ because $6 + 6 < 4 + 10$.
- **D)** If the wage rises to $w = 600\text{ NOK/hour}$, the isocost lines become flatter.

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 2)
> **Correct Option: B)**
> - **Slope**: $-\frac{w}{p} = -\frac{400}{200} = \mathbf{-2.0}$.
> - **Cost check**: $C(A) = 400(4) + 200(10) = 1,600 + 2,000 = \mathbf{3,600\text{ NOK}}$; $C(B) = 400(6) + 200(6) = 2,400 + 1,200 = \mathbf{3,600\text{ NOK}}$ ($R = 18 - 2L$).Neither dominates the other because $A$ uses less labour while $B$ uses less energy.

### Question 3 — Topic 3 (Optimal Choice: $MRS$ vs. $MRT$)
A worker with hourly wage $w = 300\text{ NOK/hour}$ is currently choosing $14\text{ hours}$ of free time ($10\text{ hours}$ of work) and $3,000\text{ NOK}$ of consumption. At this bundle, her Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$) between free time and consumption is $450\text{ NOK}$. To maximize her utility, what should she do?
- **A)** Keep working $10\text{ hours}$, because $3,000 / 10 = 300 = w$.
- **B)** Work more hours (reduce free time), because $MRS > MRT$.
- **C)** Work fewer hours (increase free time), because she values an extra hour of free time ($450\text{ NOK}$) at more than its market opportunity cost ($MRT = 300\text{ NOK}$).
- **D)** Work more hours, because the substitution effect always dominates when $MRS = 450$.

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 3)
> **Correct Option: C)**
> - At $(t=14, c=3000)$, $MRS = 450 > MRT = w = 300$. She is willing to give up $450\text{ NOK}$ of consumption to gain $1\text{ hour}$ of free time, whereas the market only requires her to give up $300\text{ NOK}$ in wage income. Moving right along the budget line (**more free time, less work**) increases her utility until $MRS$ falls to $300$.

### Question 4 — Topic 5 (Competitive Markets: Shifts vs. Movements Along)
In a competitive market for Norwegian strawberries, which of the following events will cause a **rightward shift of the demand curve** for strawberries?
- **A)** A fall in the market price of strawberries due to good summer weather.
- **B)** A subsidy paid to strawberry farmers that lowers their marginal cost of picking berries.
- **C)** A sharp increase in the price of raspberries (a substitute for strawberries) together with higher household incomes.
- **D)** The introduction of new harvesting robots on strawberry farms.

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 4)
> **Correct Option: C)**
> - A change in the price of strawberries (**A**) causes a **movement along** the demand curve. Farmer subsidies (**B**) and harvesting robots (**D**) lower marginal cost and shift the **supply curve** right. Higher price of a substitute (raspberries) and higher income (**C**) shift the **demand curve** right.

### Question 5 — Topic 6 (Labour Market Statistics Trap)
In an economy with a working-age population of $2,000,000$, there are $1,300,000$ employed workers and $100,000$ unemployed workers. Suppose $100,000$ previously inactive students graduate and enter the labour force: $60,000$ immediately start jobs and $40,000$ are actively searching for work. What happens to the **employment rate** and the **unemployment rate**?
- **A)** The employment rate increases from $65.0\%$ to $68.0\%$, and the unemployment rate **also increases** from $7.14\%$ to $9.33\%$.
- **B)** Since the employment rate increases by $3.0$ percentage points, the unemployment rate must fall by $3.0$ percentage points.
- **C)** Both the employment rate and the unemployment rate decrease because the labour force is larger.
- **D)** The employment rate increases from $92.86\%$ to $90.67\%$.

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 5)
> **Correct Option: A)**
> - **Initial state**: $\text{Labour Force}_0 = 1,300\text{k} + 100\text{k} = 1,400\text{k}$.
>   $$\text{Employment Rate}_0 = \frac{1,300\text{k}}{2,000\text{k}} = \mathbf{65.0\%}, \qquad \text{Unemployment Rate}_0 = \frac{100\text{k}}{1,400\text{k}} = \mathbf{7.14\%}$$
> - **New state**: $\text{Employed}_1 = 1,360\text{k}$, $\text{Unemployed}_1 = 140\text{k}$, $\text{Labour Force}_1 = 1,500\text{k}$.
>   $$\text{Employment Rate}_1 = \frac{1,360\text{k}}{2,000\text{k}} = \mathbf{68.0\%} \ (\uparrow), \qquad \text{Unemployment Rate}_1 = \frac{140\text{k}}{1,500\text{k}} = \mathbf{9.33\%} \ (\uparrow)$$

### Question 6 — Topics 6 & 9 (WS–PS Model & Equilibrium Real Wage)
In the macroeconomic WS–PS model, which of the following changes will **increase the equilibrium real wage ($w^*$)** in the economy?
- **A)** A reduction in the disutility of effort due to better workplace ergonomics.
- **B)** An increase in the unemployment benefit replacement rate from $62\%$ to $75\%$.
- **C)** Coordinated wage restraint via the Norwegian *frontfag* model.
- **D)** The entry of new competing firms in the product market (or an increase in labour productivity $\lambda$).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Explanation (Question 6)
> **Correct Option: D)**
> - Options **A**, **B**, and **C** all shift the **upward-sloping WS curve** (changing equilibrium employment $N^*$ while leaving the equilibrium real wage unchanged along the horizontal PS curve). Only **D** shifts the **horizontal PS curve upward** ($w^{PS} = \lambda(1-\sigma)$), increasing **both** the equilibrium real wage $w^*$ and employment $N^*$.

## Part 2: Short-Answer & Numerical Practice (Max 200 words each)

### Question 7 — Topic 2: Opportunity Cost & Economic Rent (`Spring 2025 Part 2 Q1` Style)
You have won a free, non-refundable ticket to an outdoor concert this Saturday afternoon, which gives you a subjective enjoyment benefit of $900\text{ NOK}$, but standing in the rain has a discomfort cost of $150\text{ NOK}$. Your best alternative use of Saturday afternoon is working an extra shift at a café, which pays $800\text{ NOK}$ in wages and has an effort disutility of $250\text{ NOK}$.
1. What is the **opportunity cost** and the **economic cost** of attending the concert?
2. What is the **economic rent** of attending the concert, and should you go?

> [!question]- Show Model Answer (Question 7 — 118 words)
> 1. **Net value of each option**:
>    - **Concert (chosen option A)**: $\text{Benefit } (900\text{ NOK}) - \text{Direct discomfort cost } (150\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{750\text{ NOK}}$.
>    - **Working at the café (reservation option B)**: $\text{Wage } (800\text{ NOK}) - \text{Effort disutility } (250\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{550\text{ NOK}}$.
>    - The **opportunity cost** of attending the concert is the net value of the best foregone alternative (working at the café): **$550\text{ NOK}$**.
>    - The **economic cost** of attending the concert is the sum of its direct cost and opportunity cost: $150\text{ NOK} + 550\text{ NOK} = \mathbf{700\text{ NOK}}$.
> 2. **Economic rent and decision**:
>    $$\text{Economic Rent} = \text{Net Value}(\text{Concert}) - \text{Opportunity Cost} = 750 - 550 = \mathbf{200\text{ NOK}} \quad (= 900 - 700)$$
>    Because the economic rent is strictly positive ($+200\text{ NOK} > 0$), **yes, you should attend the concert**.

### Question 8 — Topic 4: Numerical Employment Rent & No-Shirking Wage (`Fall 2025` / `V2026` / `Lecture 11` Style)
Sofia works $37.5\text{ hours per week}$ at an hourly wage of $160\text{ NOK/hour}$. Her disutility of work effort is $25\text{ NOK/hour}$. If she loses her job, she receives unemployment benefits of $65\text{ NOK/hour}$ and experiences a psychological cost of being unemployed equal to $15\text{ NOK/hour}$. She evaluates her situation over a $120\text{-week}$ horizon and expects it to take **$32\text{ weeks}$** to find a new, identical job.
1. Calculate Sofia's **employment rent per hour** and her **total employment rent**.
2. Suppose instead that we measure payoffs weekly: Sofia's weekly reservation wage is $w_r = 6,000\text{ NOK}$, weekly effort cost is $c = 1,200\text{ NOK}$, her planning horizon is $h = 80\text{ weeks}$, and a shirking worker is caught and fired after $s = 20\text{ weeks}$. Calculate the firm's minimum **no-shirking weekly wage $w^{NS}$**.

> [!question]- Show Model Answer (Question 8 — 145 words)
> 1. **Sofia's Employment Rent**:
>    - **Net hourly value when employed**: $w - c = 160 - 25 = \mathbf{135\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
>    - **Net hourly value when unemployed**: $b - s = 65 - 15 = \mathbf{50\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
>    - **Employment rent per hour**: $135 - 50 = \mathbf{85\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
>    - **Expected hours of unemployment**: $37.5\text{ hours/week} \times 32\text{ weeks} = \mathbf{1,200\text{ hours}}$ *(weeks 33–120 are identical in both states and do not affect the cost of job loss)*.
>    - **Total Employment Rent**: $85\text{ NOK/hour} \times 1,200\text{ hours} = \mathbf{102,000\text{ NOK}}$.
> 2. **Minimum No-Shirking Weekly Wage ($w^{NS}$)**:
>    Equating the effort cost saved during the $s = 20$ weeks of shirking ($\text{Area A} = c \cdot s$) with the employment rent lost during the remaining $h - s = 60$ weeks ($\text{Area B} = (w - c - w_r)(h - s)$):
>    $$w^{NS} = w_r + c + \left(\frac{s}{h - s}\right)c = 6,000 + 1,200 + \left(\frac{20}{80 - 20}\right)(1,200) = 7,200 + 400 = \mathbf{7,600\text{ NOK/week}}$$

### Question 9 — Topic 8: Value-Added GDP & Two Recession Definitions (`Topic 8 Ex. 1–3` Style)
In a small island economy with no government ($G=0$), fisherfolk catch fish worth $20\text{ million NOK}$ using $0$ intermediate inputs and sell all the fish to local restaurants. The restaurants buy $20\text{ million NOK}$ of fish and $5\text{ million NOK}$ of electricity (produced domestically with $0$ inputs) and sell meals worth $70\text{ million NOK}$ exclusively to foreign cruise tourists.
1. Calculate the economy's **GDP** using the value-added method and state the size of **Exports ($X$)**.
2. Suppose a volcanic eruption permanently destroys half of the island's fishing grounds, permanently lowering the economy's output level by $30\%$. Is the island in a permanent recession under **Definition 1** and **Definition 2** of a recession?

> [!question]- Show Model Answer (Question 9 — 152 words)
> 1. **Value-Added GDP and Exports**:
>    - **Fisherfolk value added**: $20 - 0 = 20\text{ mill. NOK}$.
>    - **Electricity value added**: $5 - 0 = 5\text{ mill. NOK}$.
>    - **Restaurants value added**: $70 - (20 + 5) = 45\text{ mill. NOK}$.
>    - **Total GDP**: $\sum \text{Value Added} = 20 + 5 + 45 = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$ (which equals the market value of final meals sold to end-users, avoiding double counting of fish and electricity).
>    - Because all meals are sold to foreign tourists, **Exports $X = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$**.
> 2. **Recession Definitions**:
>    - **Definition 1 (Output is declining / negative growth)**: The economy is in a recession **only during the transition period while GDP is actively falling** by $30\%$; once output stabilizes at the lower level, the recession is over.
>    - **Definition 2 (Output is below its normal/potential level)**: **No**, it is not a permanent recession because the volcanic eruption permanently reduced the island's productive capacity—the $30\%$ lower output is the economy's **"new normal"**.

### Question 10 — Topic 9: Conflicting Claims & the Wage–Price Spiral (`V2026 Exam Part 2 Q3` Style)
Using the wage-setting and price-setting (WS–PS) model, explain how **persistent inflation** can arise from **conflicting claims on output** when aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low, and explain how an increase in unemployment dampens inflation. *(Max 200 words)*

> [!question]- Show Model Answer (Question 10 — 158 words)
> In the WS–PS model, each worker produces $\lambda$ units of output, which is divided between the worker's real wage ($w$) and the firm's profit per worker ($\lambda - w$). The horizontal **PS curve** represents the real wage $w^{PS} = \lambda(1-\sigma)$ consistent with firms' profit-maximizing price markup $\sigma$, while the upward-sloping **WS curve** shows the real wage $w^{WS}$ needed to motivate workers at each employment level.
>
> When aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low ($N > N^*$), the WS curve lies **above** the PS curve ($w^{WS} > w^{PS}$). There are **conflicting claims**: workers' real wage demands plus firms' target profit share exceed $100\%$ of output per worker $\lambda$ (a positive **bargaining gap**). Low unemployment reduces the cost of job loss, forcing firms to raise **nominal wages ($W \uparrow$)** to recruit and retain workers. Higher wage costs squeeze profit margins, so firms respond by raising **prices ($P \uparrow$)** to restore their markup $\sigma$. This erodes the real wage back to $w^{PS}$, triggering a continuous **wage–price spiral**.
>
> Higher unemployment increases workers' fear of job loss (employment rent), weakening nominal wage demands and shrinking the bargaining gap, which slows cost and price growth (**disinflation**).

## Part 3: Comprehensive Analytical Tasks (`a–e`, 10 points each)

### Question 11 — Topics 6 & 7: The WS–PS Model, Trade Unions, Norwegian *Frontfag* & Lorenz Inequality (`Fall 2024` + `Fall 2025` + `Lecture 13` Synthesis)
Consider the macroeconomic WS–PS diagram where the horizontal axis measures Employment $N$ (with a vertical line at the Labour Force $L = 90\%$) and the vertical axis measures the Real Wage $w = W/P$ (with a horizontal dashed line at output per worker $\lambda = 100$ and a horizontal Price-Setting curve at $w^{PS} = 60$). The Wage-Setting curve $WS_0$ intersects $PS$ at **Point A** ($N^* = 80\%, w^* = 60$).
- **a)** Define the **labour force** and explain why the wage-setting ($WS$) curve is upward-sloping.
- **b)** Explain why **Point A** is the equilibrium in the labour market, and explain why firms do not cut the wage below $w^* = 60$ even though $10\%$ of the working-age population ($10$ out of $90$ in the labour force) is unemployed.
- **c)** Distinguish between a trade union's **bargaining (strike-threat) effect** and its **voice (motivation) effect** in the WS–PS diagram. How can the **Norwegian model of coordinated wage formation (*frontfagsmodellen*)** be illustrated in this diagram, and does it lead to a higher equilibrium real wage?
- **d)** Suppose new competing firms enter the product market, reducing firms' profit markup $\sigma$ from $0.40$ to $0.30$. Explain how this affects the WS–PS equilibrium.
- **e)** Show how the initial equilibrium at Point A ($10$ unemployed, $80$ workers earning a $60\%$ wage share, $10$ owners earning a $40\%$ profit share) is mapped onto a **Lorenz curve**, and explain how the increase in product-market competition from **part (d)** shifts the Lorenz curve and affects the **Gini coefficient**.

> [!question]- Show Complete Model Solution (Question 11 `a–e`)
> - **a) Labour Force & Upward-Sloping WS Curve**:
>   - The **labour force** consists of all working-age individuals who are either **employed** or **unemployed** (without work, available to start within 2 weeks, and actively seeking work during the last 4 weeks). It excludes economically inactive groups such as full-time students, retirees, disability recipients, and stay-at-home parents.
>   - The **WS curve slopes upward** because as aggregate employment $N$ increases (moving right), the unemployment rate $u$ falls. With fewer unemployed people competing for vacancies, a dismissed worker can find a new job much faster. This reduces the expected duration of unemployment, raises the worker's reservation wage, and **reduces the cost of job loss (employment rent)**. To prevent shirking and motivate effort, employers must offer a higher real wage $w$.
> - **b) Why Point A Is the Nash Equilibrium & Why Firms Do Not Cut Wages**:
>   - At **Point A $(N^*=80, w^*=60)$**, the real wage required to motivate workers to exert effort ($w^{WS} = 60$) equals the real wage resulting from firms' profit-maximizing price-setting ($w^{PS} = 60$). Neither workers/HR departments nor pricing departments have an incentive to change wages, prices, or employment.
>   - Even though unemployed workers would gladly accept a job below $w^* = 60$, firms **will not cut wages below Point A** because paying less than $w^{WS}$ destroys the employment rent required to discipline existing workers—workers would shirk, reducing labour productivity and lowering firm profits.
> - **c) Union Bargaining vs. Voice Effects & Norwegian *Frontfagsmodellen***:
>   - **Bargaining (strike-threat) effect**: If a union uses its strike threat to demand a wage above the minimum no-shirking wage, the **WS curve shifts upward**. Firms respond to higher nominal wage costs by raising prices $P$ to protect their markup $\sigma$, leaving the equilibrium real wage unchanged at $w^* = 60$ while **reducing employment** ($N^* \downarrow, u^* \uparrow$).
>   - **Voice (motivation) effect**: When constructive union–employer dialogue improves working conditions and makes workers feel respected, the disutility of effort falls, **shifting the WS curve downward** and **increasing employment** ($N^* \uparrow$).
>   - **Norwegian *Frontfagsmodellen***: In Norway, wage negotiations start in the internationally exposed export manufacturing sector (*frontfaget*), which sets a binding norm for the sheltered and public sectors. Because coordinated confederations (LO/NHO) internalize the macroeconomic threat of losing export competitiveness and causing unemployment, they exercise wage restraint—illustrated as a **downward shift of the WS curve**. Because $w^*$ is fixed by the horizontal PS curve, coordination does **not** directly yield a higher real wage; instead, it achieves **higher equilibrium employment and lower structural unemployment**.
> - **d) Effect of Stronger Product-Market Competition ($\sigma: 0.40 \to 0.30$)**:
>   - Stronger competition reduces firms' market power and lowers their profit markup $\sigma$ from $0.40$ to $0.30$. Firms charge lower prices $P$ relative to nominal wages $W$, which **shifts the horizontal PS curve upward** from $w_1^{PS} = 100(1 - 0.40) = 60$ to $w_2^{PS} = 100(1 - 0.30) = \mathbf{70}$ (while the WS curve is unchanged).
>   - The economy moves up and right along $WS_0$ to a new equilibrium $E_2$: **both the equilibrium real wage ($60 \to 70$) and equilibrium employment ($80 \to 82.9$) increase**, while unemployment falls ($10 \to 7.1$).
> - **e) Mapping to the Lorenz Curve & Gini Inequality**:
>   - Ordering the $100$ individuals from poorest to richest, the baseline Lorenz curve starts at $(0,0)$, stays flat along the horizontal axis to **Kink 1 at $(10\%, 0\%)$** (the $10$ unemployed with zero market income), rises linearly across the $80$ employed workers to **Kink 2 at $(90\%, 60\%)$** (since the first $90\%$ of the population earns the $60\%$ wage share), and rises steeply across the $10$ owners to $(100\%, 100\%)$.
>   - When stronger competition shifts the PS curve up in **part (d)**, unemployment falls from $10$ to $7.1$ (**Kink 1 shifts left to $(7.1\%, 0\%)$**) and the wage share rises from $60\%$ to $70\%$ (**Kink 2 shifts vertically up to $(90\%, 70\%)$**). The entire Lorenz curve shifts **inward toward the $45^\circ$ line of perfect equality**, shrinking Area $A$ and **reducing the Gini coefficient $G = A/(A+B)$ (lower income inequality)**.

### Question 12 — Topic 5: Competitive Market Equilibrium, Surplus & Cost/Tariff Shock (`Lecture 11 Prob. 2` + `V2026 Part 3` Synthesis)
Consider a competitive market for artisan coffee beans where individual roasters are price-takers. At the initial market equilibrium $E_0$, the equilibrium price is $P_0 = 200\text{ NOK/kg}$ and the equilibrium quantity is $Q_0 = 50,000\text{ kg/week}$. The maximum Willingness to Pay on the linear demand curve $D$ is $P_{\max}^D = 400\text{ NOK/kg}$, and the minimum marginal cost on the linear market supply curve $S_0$ is $P_{\min}^S = 100\text{ NOK/kg}$.
- **a)** Explain what it means that roasters are **price-takers**, and explain why each roaster chooses to produce the quantity where $P = MC$.
- **b)** Calculate **Consumer Surplus ($CS$)**, **Producer Surplus ($PS$)**, and **Total Surplus ($TS$)** at $E_0$, and explain why $E_0$ is **Pareto efficient**.
- **c)** What is the marginal cost of the $50,000\text{th}$ kilogram of coffee before any tax? Suppose a new $20\%$ import tariff on raw green coffee beans increases every roaster's marginal cost by $20\%$ at every output level. What is the new marginal cost of supplying $Q_0 = 50,000\text{ kg}$, and how will roasters react if the market price temporarily remains at $200\text{ NOK/kg}$?
- **d)** Explain how the $20\%$ cost increase shifts the curves in the supply-and-demand diagram and establishes a new equilibrium $E_1 (Q_1, P_1)$.
- **e)** Will the new equilibrium price $P_1$ be equal to, higher than, or lower than $240\text{ NOK/kg}$? Explain your answer and state how the steepness (price elasticity) of the demand curve affects the size of the price increase.

> [!question]- Show Complete Model Solution (Question 12 `a–e`)
> - **a) Price-Taking Behaviour & $P = MC$ Rule**:
>   - Because many small roasters sell a homogeneous product alongside many buyers, no single roaster can influence the market price $P_0 = 200\text{ NOK/kg}$—each takes $P_0$ as given.
>   - If $P > MC(q)$, roasting one additional kilogram adds $P$ to revenue and only $MC$ to cost, increasing profit by $P - MC > 0$. If $P < MC(q)$, the last kilogram costs more to produce than it sells for, reducing profit. Profit is therefore maximized where **$P = MC(q)$**, making the upward-sloping $MC$ curve the firm's (and market's) supply curve.
> - **b) Surplus Calculations & Pareto Efficiency**:
>   $$\begin{aligned}
>   CS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 50,000 \times (400 - 200) = \mathbf{5,000,000\text{ NOK/week}} \\
>   PS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 50,000 \times (200 - 100) = \mathbf{2,500,000\text{ NOK/week}} \\
>   TS &= CS + PS = \mathbf{7,500,000\text{ NOK/week}}
>   \end{aligned}$$
>   $E_0$ is **Pareto efficient** because all potential trades where a buyer's $\text{WTP} \ge \text{seller's } MC$ are carried out (up to $Q_0 = 50,000$), maximizing Total Surplus with zero Deadweight Loss ($DWL = 0$).
> - **c) Marginal Cost at $Q_0 = 50,000$ Before and After the $20\%$ Tariff**:
>   - Since $P_0 = MC_0(Q_0)$ at competitive equilibrium, the marginal cost of the $50,000\text{th}$ kg before the tariff is **$200\text{ NOK/kg}$**.
>   - A $20\%$ cost increase raises the marginal cost at $Q_0 = 50,000$ to $200 \times 1.20 = \mathbf{240\text{ NOK/kg}}$.
>   - If the market price stays at $200\text{ NOK/kg}$, then $MC_1 = 240 > P_0 = 200$: roasters lose money on the marginal kilograms and **reduce quantity supplied**.
> - **d) Curve Shift & New Equilibrium $E_1$**:
>   - The $20\%$ increase in marginal cost shifts the **market supply curve upward/leftward** from $S_0$ to $S_1 = 1.20\,MC_0$ (while the demand curve $D$ does not shift). At the old price $P_0 = 200$, excess demand emerges, bidding the price up and moving consumers up and left along $D$ until a new equilibrium $E_1(Q_1, P_1)$ is reached with **lower quantity ($Q_1 < 50,000$)** and **higher price ($P_1 > 200$)**.
> - **e) Why $P_1 < 240\text{ NOK/kg}$ & Role of Demand Steepness**:
>   - The new equilibrium price $P_1$ will be **strictly lower than $240\text{ NOK/kg}$** ($200 < P_1 < 240$). Because the demand curve slopes downward, consumers reduce their quantity demanded as price rises ($Q_1 < 50,000$). Because the supply ($MC$) curve slopes upward, producing a smaller quantity $Q_1$ lowers marginal cost along $S_1$ below $240\text{ NOK/kg}$. (With the exact linear curves $P^D = 400 - 0.004Q$ and $P^{S_1} = 120 + 0.0024Q$, $P_1 = \mathbf{225\text{ NOK/kg}}$ and $Q_1 = \mathbf{43,750\text{ kg}}$.)
>   - **Steepness rule**: The **steeper (less price-elastic)** the demand curve, the less quantity demanded falls and the **closer $P_1$ rises toward the full $240\text{ NOK/kg}$**.
